title: Growing up, in members' own words · AquaTerra
description: Essays by AquaTerra members on childhood, the end of school, friendships and being a teenager doing real work. Read the pieces, then see the drives.
lede: Growing up, in our own words is a set of essays by AquaTerra members, published on the site, about childhood, the last day at school, friendships and being left out of the photo. Several look back at being young, and a few look at what teenagers can do in Kolkata while they are still growing up.

sections.heading: looking back at being young
body: People in the Mirror starts with a girl who brought her Barbie everywhere, even to the bathroom, and looks at the many people we have been in the mirror since. The Joy of Little Things looks back to childhood, when happiness was simple and lived in finishing homework before sunset.

Syntax Error takes the words we learn as children, sorry and love and I'm fine, and says that growing up adds a question mark to each one. The Last Walk is about a final day in a school corridor, with the stale canteen bread, the old bathrooms and the high ceilings that once felt endless. It is short, and the small details carry it.

sections.heading: being in the photo, and the noise
body: When You Are Not in the Group Photo starts with a scroll through social media and a picture of friends laughing together, and the moment you realise you were not there. Almost But Not Quite looks at a group that goes out in pairs, with one person always the only single one.

Lost in the Noise says everything feels loud now, with notifications, opinions and expectations drowning out what you believe. The Curse on Society writes about child labour as a cycle still trapping millions of children, and asks readers to notice it on any street.

sections.heading: teenagers doing the work
body: Teen-Led NGO starts from the picture most people have of social impact, suited-up adults and big organisations, and asks what it looks like when the people doing the work are teenagers. That is the everyday version of AquaTerra: students who plan a drive, run it and write it up.

The pieces are easier to read next to the work they describe. [Student leadership](/impact/student-leadership) explains how students run AquaTerra, [volunteering for teenagers](/impact/volunteering-for-teens-in-kolkata) covers what teens can do in Kolkata, and [what a student-run NGO is](/impact/what-is-a-student-run-ngo) sets out the idea.

learnings: Looking back at school tends to start with small things: the canteen bread, the corridor, the photo you were not in.
Being a teenager and doing real work at the same time is a theme the members keep returning to.
The essays keep both the quiet feeling of being left out and the loud pressure of being noticed.
A small detail, like a school bathroom or a group photo, can carry a whole essay.

faqs.q: What is Growing up, in our own words?
faqs.a: It is a set of essays by AquaTerra members about childhood, school, friendships and being a teenager. The pieces are published on the site under Groundwork Diaries, and they look back at being young as well as at teenagers doing real work.

faqs.q: Who writes the essays on growing up?
faqs.a: AquaTerra's members write them in their own words, and they are published on the site under Groundwork Diaries.

faqs.q: What topics do the essays on growing up cover?
faqs.a: They cover childhood memories, the last day of school, friendships and the photos people are left out of, feeling loud or quiet, and what teenagers can do in a community organisation.

faqs.q: Where can I read about teenagers running a charity in Kolkata?
faqs.a: The student leadership page explains how students run AquaTerra, and the page on volunteering for teenagers covers what teens can do in Kolkata. Both sit beside these essays in the library.
